title: Threads and std::jthread
summary: A **thread** is an independent path of execution; several can run at the same time on different processor cores. `std::thread` starts one and must be joined. `std::jthread` (C++20) joins automatically and supports **cooperative cancellation** through `std::stop_token`. Both are in `<thread>`.
ideas:
1. Start four threads that each print their id five times. Run it several times. Is the order the same?
2. Implement `parallelSum` and, in a Release build, time it against a single thread for 100 million integers.
3. Write a `jthread` spinner animation that stops when the user presses Enter.

cards.q: What happens if a joinable `std::thread` is destroyed?
cards.a:
`std::terminate` is called

A `std::thread` must be joined or detached before destruction. `std::jthread` joins automatically in its destructor.

cards.q: How do you pass an argument to a thread by reference?
cards.a:
Wrap it in `std::ref`, and ensure the object outlives the thread

The thread constructor copies its arguments. `std::ref(x)` passes a reference wrapper instead, and `x` must live long enough.

A thread killed mid-update could leave a lock held or data broken

`request_stop()` only sets a flag. The thread checks its `std::stop_token` and finishes cleanly.

cards.q: Why is `parallelSum` free of data races?
cards.a:
No thread writes anything that another thread reads or writes

Sharing read-only data and writing to separate elements needs no locks. The results are combined after the threads join.
